title: Electrician Salary Melbourne: Award Rates, Annual Pay, and Tax Guide
description: Find the electrician salary Melbourne based on Fair Work award rates. Learn how to convert hourly to annual, plus tax, super, and casual loading explained.
salarySummary: A qualified electrician (Grade 5) in Melbourne earns $32.19 per hour under the Electrical Award, equating to about $63,607 per year for a 38-hour week.

faqs.q: How is casual loading applied to an electrician's hourly rate?
faqs.a: Under the Electrical, Electronic and Communications Contracting Award 2020, casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the ordinary hourly rate. For a Grade 5 electrician, the ordinary rate is $32.19, so the casual rate becomes $40.24 per hour. This loading replaces entitlements like annual leave and sick leave.

faqs.q: What superannuation is paid on an electrician's salary?
faqs.a: Employers must pay superannuation guarantee contributions of 12% of ordinary earnings on top of the base salary. For a Grade 5 electrician earning $63,607 per year, that adds about $7,633 to the total package, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week, then by 52 weeks. For a full-time electrician working 38 hours per week at $32.19/hour: $32.19 × 38 × 52 = $63,607.44. This assumes the same rate every week with no overtime or allowances.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the Electrician Salary Melbourne

If you're researching an **electrician salary Melbourne**, the most reliable figures come from the Fair Work Ombudsman's Electrical, Electronic and Communications Contracting Award 2020. This award sets minimum pay rates for electricians across Australia, including Melbourne. For a qualified electrician with a licence (Grade 5), the minimum hourly rate is **$32.19** as of the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026. This rate already includes industry, tool, and electrician's licence allowances.

### How to Convert Hourly to Annual Pay

The standard formula for converting an hourly wage to annual salary is:

**Hourly rate × hours per week × 52 weeks**

For a full-time electrician working 38 ordinary hours per week (the standard under the award), the calculation is:

$32.19 × 38 × 52 = **$63,607.44 per year**

This is the gross annual salary before tax and super. The award defines a full-time employee as working an average of 38 hours per week, so we use that figure. If you work fewer hours, adjust accordingly.

### Fortnightly Pay

Most electricians are paid weekly or fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, multiply your weekly pay by two. For a Grade 5 electrician:

- Weekly: $1,223.11 (from the pay guide)
- Fortnightly: $2,446.22

Your employer may pay according to actual hours worked each week or an average, as allowed under clause 17.1 of the award.

### Award Rates vs National Minimum Wage

The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. An electrician's award rate is significantly higher because it reflects the skill, training, and industry allowances required. The award also includes specific classifications from Grade 1 to Grade 10, with Grade 5 being a common level for a licensed electrician. You can find the full classification table in the pay guides from Fair Work.

### Casual Loading

If you work as a casual electrician, you are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the ordinary hourly rate. This is paid instead of annual leave, personal leave, and other entitlements. For a Grade 5 casual:

- Ordinary rate: $32.19
- Casual rate: $32.19 × 1.25 = **$40.24 per hour**

Always enter your base hourly rate without casual loading into a calculator, then add the loading separately. The award states that the casual loading is paid for each hour worked (clause 11.2).

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Using the 2026–27 Australian resident tax rates:

- Tax-free threshold: $0 – $18,200
- 15%: $18,201 – $45,000
- 30%: $45,001 – $135,000
- 37%: $135,001 – $190,000
- 45%: above $190,000

For an annual salary of $63,607:

- Tax on first $18,200: $0
- Tax on next $26,800 (15%): $4,020
- Tax on remaining $18,607 (30%): $5,582.10
- Total tax: $9,602.10
- Medicare levy (2%): $1,272.14
- **Total deductions: $10,874.24**
- **Estimated take-home pay: $52,733.20 per year**

This is an estimate only. Your actual tax may vary depending on HELP debts, Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. Use the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for a more detailed breakdown.

### Superannuation Paid on Top

Employers must pay superannuation guarantee contributions of 12% of your ordinary earnings. This is paid on top of your salary, not deducted from it. For a Grade 5 electrician:

- Super: 12% of $63,607 = **$7,632.84**
- Total employment cost: $71,240.28

The super guarantee applies up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. Most electricians earn well below this threshold, so the full 12% applies. For more on packaging, see [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

### Comparing with Average Earnings

The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) reported average weekly earnings for full-time adult ordinary time employees at $2,083.70 per week (May 2026). That equates to about $108,352 per year. An electrician's salary of $63,607 is below this average, but it's the minimum award rate. Many electricians earn above award through overtime, allowances, or enterprise agreements. The award provides overtime rates of 150% for the first 2 hours and 200% thereafter for full-time employees, which can significantly boost annual income.

### Key Points to Remember

- Always use the award classification that matches your role and qualifications.
- The 38-hour week is the standard for full-time employees under the award.
- Casual loading is 25% on top of the ordinary rate, not included in the base rate.
- Super is paid on top of your salary at 12%.
- Tax estimates are based on 2026–27 rates and do not include HELP or surcharges.

For a quick reference to all minimum rates, see the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page. If you need to calculate your own pay, use the [timesheet](/).
